title: A multi-file event-driven application
lead: Assemble a planner core from an interface, implementation, adapter and separate test driver.
why: include/model.hpp declares Board, src/model.cpp implements its rules and main.cpp translates input into commands and output. Both cpp files need the header, while ordinary function definitions belong in the implementation. pragma once prevents repeated header inclusion within one translation unit; it does not repair repeated definitions across multiple translation units.
objectives: Name the responsibilities of the three files.
Build the laboratory from two translation units.
Replace vector<bool> with vector<Task> without changing results.
prerequisites: Modules 1–5: functions, STL, ownership, testing and multi-file builds.

sections.title: Files follow decision boundaries
paragraphs: include/model.hpp declares Board, src/model.cpp implements its rules and main.cpp translates input into commands and output. Both cpp files need the header, while ordinary function definitions belong in the implementation. pragma once prevents repeated header inclusion within one translation unit; it does not repair repeated definitions across multiple translation units.

A zero command adds an unfinished task and a positive number completes an existing task. Here an identifier equals its position plus one because deletion is absent. State that teaching restriction explicitly. TaskFlow uses persistent ids: if deletion were added, treating a moving position as identity could select the wrong task.

sections.title: Configuring the Studio build
paragraphs: Create a separate C++ project, add all listed files and set includeRoots to include. The application builds main.cpp and src/model.cpp. A test driver replaces main.cpp rather than adding a second main. A file inside tests does not automatically become a test; build inputs must be known and reproducible.

Work in Nexus Code Studio using a saved project copy. Verify that editing src/model.cpp changes the result instead of accidentally running an old single-file program. Removing Board::apply should produce a linker error; perform this diagnostic experiment in a copy, then restore the source and verify a successful run.

sections.title: Repeatable operations and limits
paragraphs: Board holds at most eight tasks and rejects a ninth addition. Repeating complete for an already completed task succeeds and leaves it completed. done is derived from the model rather than counted from successful commands; otherwise repeatedly completing one task could incorrectly make the completed count exceed the total.

The example uses vector<bool> only for flags; its elements have a special proxy type. We neither obtain bool& nor take an element address. If additional fields are needed, use vector<Task> while preserving the public contract. This storage refactoring should retain the same behavioural test results.

sections.title: From a model project to a graphical project
paragraphs: Retain a README describing commands and limits, sources and a verification table. Separately explain how a GUI would create a command from user interaction while keeping Board independent of Qt. Do not put QApplication or QFile into model.hpp for convenience: doing so makes model tests depend on a graphical SDK and weakens portability.

The next lessons use a real TaskFlow application in Project Studio. It extends the teaching Board with titles, persistent ids, NXTF1 data and file artifacts. What transfers is the architectural principle and tested contract, rather than a mechanical renaming of symbols. Independent work must add a requirement and test, not merely rename a finished example.

sections.title: Laboratory contract: input to observation
paragraphs: Read n=0…12 and n integer commands. Zero adds a task, up to eight. A positive value completes the existing id=position+1. Repeated completion succeeds without increasing done again. Other commands are rejected. Incomplete or trailing input produces invalid.

Trace the first reference scenario before running. Exact stdin: "4 0 0 1 1". Expected stdout: "tasks 2 done 1 rejected 0\n" Relate each algorithm step to state changes, distinguishing rejection from the point where a change is committed.

sections.title: Reading a working example
paragraphs: Command stores a delta. update receives its data explicitly. Three plus four yields seven without a global dependency. First identify data, ownership and the observable outcome. Then change exactly one initial condition and predict which observation changes. This connects syntax to a contract rather than memorizing finished source text.

The first complete sets true. The second leaves true. Counting state must not count two completed tasks. Compare the second example with the first: what new boundary is covered, and which test distinguishes the correct implementation from a superficially similar mistake? Retain both sources, predictions and actual observations so that the explanation can be reproduced.

sections.title: Independent checking and transfer
paragraphs: Replace vector<bool> with vector<Task> without changing results. Retain a checkable result: Replace vector<bool> with vector<Task> without changing results. Explain the selected contract and supply an independent example. Begin with a specification and input bounds; the worked function is a scaffold, not the requirements of another domain. State an independent expectation before execution so that a test is not fitted to accidental output.

Add deletion with stable ids and an independent test. Retain a checkable result: Add deletion with stable ids and an independent test. Explain the selected contract and supply an independent example. Record decisions, a rejected alternative, checked scenarios and remaining limitations. Ask a reviewer for a small requirement change and explain which files, tests and observations it should affect.

sections.title: Checking a boundary rejection
paragraphs: Read n=0…12 and n integer commands. Zero adds a task, up to eight. A positive value completes the existing id=position+1. Repeated completion succeeds without increasing done again. Other commands are rejected. Incomplete or trailing input produces invalid. The last reference case distinguishes a permitted command from a malformed protocol. Identify where rejection starts and which fields must remain unchanged.

Analyze this reference case: {"stdin":"0 x","stdout":"invalid\n"} Then change one boundary and state the new expectation before running. Compare the correct solution with a safe mutation in a project copy; the test must detect the behavioural change rather than merely report a successful build.

assessment.question: Which translation units build the application?
assessment.explanation: The header is included and model definitions are linked separately.

assessment.question: How does repeated complete affect done?
answers: It does not increase it again.
assessment.explanation: The task state is already true.

assessment.question: Why use stable ids when deleting?
answers: So list position is not confused with task identity.

readinessCheck.question: What is required when an operation with a strong guarantee fails?
readinessCheck.explanation: The guarantee concerns the specified model at an operation boundary.

readinessCheck.question: Who owns an object supplied through an ordinary reference?
answers: Ownership is specified separately; a reference does not transfer it.
readinessCheck.explanation: The owner must outlive use of the reference.

readinessCheck.question: How is a driver with its own main built?
answers: Instead of application main, sharing model sources.
readinessCheck.explanation: The application and driver have separate entry points and builds.

Add deletion with stable ids and an independent test.
